body:
Why chemists use the mole

Even a small sample of a substance contains an enormous number of atoms or molecules. Counting them individually is impractical. The mole provides a convenient way to express the amount of a substance in terms of the number of specified particles.

The mole, symbol mol, is the SI unit of amount of substance. One mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 1023 specified elementary entities.

These entities may be atoms, molecules, ions or other specified particles. The number of entities in 1 mole is called the Avogadro number. Its corresponding constant is represented by NA.

For school-level calculations, the exact value is usually rounded to 6.022 × 1023 particles per mole.

The modern SI definition based on a fixed Avogadro constant took effect on 20 May 2019. Earlier textbooks may describe 1 mole as the amount containing as many particles as there are atoms in 12 g of carbon-12. That historical definition was replaced, but it leads to the same practical school-level numerical results.

Molar mass connects mass and amount

The molar mass of a substance is the mass of 1 mole of its specified particles. It is expressed in grams per mole, written g/mol.

For ordinary school calculations, the numerical value of molar mass in g/mol is the same as the corresponding atomic, molecular or formula unit mass in u.

  • Atomic mass of hydrogen is approximately 1 u; molar mass of hydrogen atoms is approximately 1 g/mol.
  • Molecular mass of water is approximately 18 u; molar mass of water molecules is approximately 18 g/mol.
  • Molecular mass of oxygen gas, O2, is approximately 32 u; molar mass of O2 molecules is approximately 32 g/mol.
  • Formula unit mass of NaCl is approximately 58.5 u; molar mass of NaCl formula units is approximately 58.5 g/mol.

Calculating moles from mass

If the mass of a sample and its molar mass are known, the number of moles can be calculated as follows:

\(n=\frac{m}{M}\)

Here, n is the amount in moles, m is the given mass in grams and M is the molar mass in g/mol.

One-step calculation

A sample contains 9 g of pure water. Since the molar mass of H2O is 18 g/mol:

\(n=\frac{9}{18}=0.5\ \mathrm{mol}\)

The sample therefore contains 0.5 mol of water molecules.

Calculating the number of particles

The number of particles is obtained by multiplying the amount in moles by the Avogadro constant:

\(N=n\times N_A\)

For example, 0.5 mol of water molecules contains approximately:

0.5 × 6.022 × 1023 = 3.011 × 1023 water molecules.

For 1 mol of water, there are 6.022 × 1023 H2O molecules. Since each molecule contains 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom, the sample contains 2 mol of hydrogen atoms and 1 mol of oxygen atoms.

Atoms and molecules must not be confused

One mole of oxygen atoms has a mass of approximately 16 g. One mole of oxygen molecules, O2, has a mass of approximately 32 g. Both contain the same number of specified entities, but one specified entity is an atom in the first case and a 2-atom molecule in the second.

Always identify the entities being counted. The statements 1 mol of O atoms and 1 mol of O2 molecules do not describe the same quantity of oxygen atoms.

Prelims focus

  • 1 mol contains exactly 6.02214076 × 1023 specified entities.
  • For basic calculations, use approximately 6.022 × 1023.
  • The modern SI definition of the mole took effect on 20 May 2019.
  • The molar mass of water is approximately 18 g/mol.
  • The molar mass of O2 is approximately 32 g/mol.
  • Trap: The mass of 1 mol of oxygen atoms is not the same as the mass of 1 mol of O2 molecules.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class IX, Chapter 3, Atoms and Molecules, section 3.5.3, 2018–19 textbook text, printed pp. 40–42; BIPM, The International System of Units, 9th edition, revised June 2026, section 2.3.5, The mole, and SI base unit: mole, consulted 3 November 2026; IUPAC Gold Book, Mole, definition and effective date, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: The Mole Concept: Counting Particles Through Mass

body:
Meaning of valency

Valency is the combining capacity of an atom or an element. It describes how an atom commonly combines with other atoms to form compounds.

For many simple compounds, valency is connected with the number of electrons an atom loses, gains or shares while attaining a stable outer electronic arrangement.

Hydrogen commonly has valency 1, oxygen has valency 2, magnesium has valency 2 and aluminium has valency 3.

In the simple school-level model, an atom with 1, 2, 3 or 4 valence electrons often shows a valency equal to that number. For 5, 6 or 7 valence electrons, a common valency is 8 minus that number. Atoms with a completely filled outermost shell generally have valency 0.

This is a useful introductory rule, not a complete prediction of every compound. Some elements exhibit variable valencies. For example, iron can form Fe2+ and Fe3+ ions, and phosphorus can show valencies 3 and 5.

Valency and ionic charge are related but different

Valency describes combining capacity and is generally written without a positive or negative sign. Ionic charge describes the net electrical charge produced when electrons are lost or gained.

Thus, a sodium ion, Na+, has charge +1; a magnesium ion, Mg2+, has charge +2; and an oxide ion, O2−, has charge −2. The corresponding simple combining valencies are 1, 2 and 2.

Common ions needed for chemical formulae

IonSymbolCharge
SodiumNa++1
PotassiumK++1
MagnesiumMg2++2
CalciumCa2++2
AluminiumAl3++3
ChlorideCl−−1
OxideO2−−2
HydroxideOH−−1
NitrateNO3−−1
CarbonateCO32−−2
SulphateSO42−−2
AmmoniumNH4++1

The rule of electrical neutrality

An ionic compound is electrically neutral overall. Its formula must therefore contain positive and negative ions in proportions that make the total positive charge equal to the total negative charge.

To write a simple ionic formula:

  1. Write the positive ion first and the negative ion second.
  2. Identify their respective charges.
  3. Choose the smallest whole-number ratio that balances the charges.
  4. Write this ratio as subscripts, omitting any subscript equal to 1.
  5. Do not include the ionic charges in the final formula of the neutral compound.

Example: magnesium chloride

Magnesium forms Mg2+, while chlorine forms Cl−. One magnesium ion requires 2 chloride ions to balance its +2 charge. The formula is therefore MgCl2.

Example: aluminium oxide

Aluminium forms Al3+, while oxygen forms O2−. Two aluminium ions contribute +6, and 3 oxide ions contribute −6. The smallest neutral ratio is therefore 2 aluminium ions to 3 oxide ions, giving Al2O3.

Example: calcium oxide

Calcium and oxide ions have charges +2 and −2. They combine in a 1:1 ratio, so the formula is CaO, not Ca2O2. Ionic formulas use the simplest whole-number ratio.

Writing formulae containing polyatomic ions

A polyatomic ion is a group of atoms that carries a charge and behaves as a single ion in many chemical formulas. The internal formula of the group must remain unchanged.

Calcium hydroxide contains Ca2+ and OH−. Since 2 hydroxide ions are required for each calcium ion, its formula is Ca(OH)2.

The brackets mean that the entire OH group occurs twice. Therefore, Ca(OH)2 contains 1 calcium atom, 2 oxygen atoms and 2 hydrogen atoms in each formula unit.

In NaOH, only 1 hydroxide group is present, so brackets are unnecessary. Other useful formulas include Na2CO3 for sodium carbonate, CaCO3 for calcium carbonate and (NH4)2SO4 for ammonium sulphate.

Prelims focus

  • Valency is the combining capacity of an element.
  • An ionic compound must be electrically neutral overall.
  • Magnesium chloride is MgCl2.
  • Aluminium oxide is Al2O3.
  • Calcium hydroxide is Ca(OH)2.
  • Trap: CaO is correct; Ca2O2 is not the simplest ionic formula.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class IX, Chapter 3, Atoms and Molecules, sections 3.3.3–3.4.1, printed pp. 36–39; NCERT, Science, Class IX, Chapter 4, Structure of the Atom, section 4.4, printed pp. 50–52.]

title: Valency, Ionic Charges and Writing Chemical Formulae

body:
Atoms are not indivisible

Dalton treated atoms as indivisible particles. Later discoveries showed that atoms contain smaller particles with different masses, charges and locations. The 3 basic subatomic particles considered at this level are electrons, protons and neutrons.

The nucleus and the surrounding electrons

At the centre of an atom is a very small, dense region called the nucleus. It contains protons and, in most atoms, neutrons. Electrons occupy the region surrounding the nucleus.

The nucleus contains nearly all the atom's mass because protons and neutrons are much more massive than electrons. Nevertheless, the nucleus occupies only a tiny fraction of the atom's overall volume.

Comparison of the 3 particles

ParticleRelative chargeApproximate massLocation
Electron−1About 1/1836 of a protonOutside nucleus
Proton+1About 1 uNucleus
Neutron0About 1 uNucleus

The proton and electron have charges equal in magnitude but opposite in sign. The neutron is electrically neutral. For most introductory calculations, electron mass can be neglected when estimating an atom's mass.

Protons and neutrons together are called nucleons.

Electrical neutrality of an atom

An ordinary neutral atom contains equal numbers of protons and electrons. Their opposite charges cancel.

For example, a neutral sodium atom contains 11 protons and 11 electrons. Its total charge is zero. When that sodium atom loses 1 electron, it becomes Na+. It still contains 11 protons, but now has only 10 electrons.

Changing the number of electrons changes the charge of an atom. It does not change the identity of the element, because the number of protons remains unchanged.

Important discoveries

J. J. Thomson identified the electron in 1897 through studies of cathode rays. Earlier, Eugen Goldstein had observed positively charged canal rays in 1886. Such findings contributed to the understanding of positive particles in matter.

Ernest Rutherford subsequently established that the hydrogen nucleus is a positively charged nuclear particle, recognised as the proton. James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932.

These discoveries gradually replaced the picture of an indivisible atom with an atom containing a nucleus and electrons.

The special case of ordinary hydrogen

The most common hydrogen isotope, called protium, contains 1 proton and no neutron. A neutral protium atom also contains 1 electron.

Thus, the statement that every atomic nucleus contains neutrons is incorrect. Protium is the familiar exception.

Prelims focus

  • Electrons carry charge −1; protons +1; neutrons 0.
  • Protons and neutrons are located in the nucleus.
  • Electrons have much smaller masses than protons and neutrons.
  • J. J. Thomson identified the electron in 1897.
  • James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932.
  • Trap: The nucleus of ordinary hydrogen-1 contains no neutron.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class IX, Chapter 4, Structure of the Atom, sections 4.1–4.2.4, printed pp. 46–49; Science History Institute, Joseph John J. J. Thomson, consulted 3 November 2026; American Institute of Physics, Rutherford and the Proton, consulted 3 November 2026; American Physical Society, May 1932: Chadwick Reports the Discovery of the Neutron, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A tiny nucleus contains protons and neutrons and nearly all atomic mass; much lighter electrons occupy the surrounding region.
pictures.caption: An atom has a tiny central nucleus and electrons occupying the surrounding region.

title: Electrons, Protons and Neutrons: The Particles Within an Atom

body:
Why models of the atom changed

An atomic model is a scientific explanation of the atom's internal structure. As scientists discovered charged particles and obtained new experimental evidence, older models had to be revised.

The progression from Thomson to Rutherford to Bohr is important because each model answered questions left unresolved by its predecessor.

Thomson's model: electrons in a positive sphere

J. J. Thomson proposed that an atom consisted of a sphere of positive charge with negatively charged electrons embedded throughout it. This is commonly called the plum-pudding model or compared with seeds embedded in a watermelon.

Thomson's model explained why atoms could be electrically neutral: the total negative charge of the electrons balanced the positive charge distributed through the atom.

However, it did not explain the later evidence that positive charge is concentrated in a very small central region.

Rutherford's model: the discovery of the nucleus

In research associated with Ernest Rutherford and the scattering observations of Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, positively charged alpha particles were directed toward a thin gold foil.

Three main observations were made:

  • Most alpha particles passed through the foil without significant deflection.
  • Some particles were deflected from their original direction.
  • A very small fraction were deflected through large angles, with some appearing to rebound.

Rutherford interpreted these observations as evidence that most of the atom is empty space, while its positive charge and nearly all its mass are concentrated in a very small central nucleus.

The Rutherford nuclear model, proposed in 1911, placed a small positively charged nucleus at the centre with electrons moving around it.

Limitation of Rutherford's model

According to classical physics, an electrically charged particle moving in a circular orbit is accelerated and should continuously radiate energy. An orbiting electron would therefore lose energy and eventually fall into the nucleus.

Actual atoms are stable. Rutherford's model could not adequately explain this stability.

Bohr's model: permitted electron energy levels

In 1913, Niels Bohr proposed a model that addressed the stability problem by introducing special permitted electron orbits, also called energy levels or shells.

The main ideas of Bohr's school-level model are:

  1. Electrons can occupy only certain permitted energy levels around the nucleus.
  2. While an electron remains in one of these permitted levels, it does not continuously radiate energy.
  3. Electrons may move between permitted levels by absorbing or emitting suitable amounts of energy.

The permitted energy levels explain why the classical prediction of continuous energy loss does not describe a stable atom.

These levels are commonly represented by the letters K, L, M, N, beginning with the innermost shell.

The shell pictures used at this level are simplified models. Electrons in modern atomic theory are not treated as miniature planets following precisely defined classical circular paths.

Comparing the models

Thomson correctly recognised the presence of electrons and explained overall electrical neutrality. Rutherford established the nuclear structure of the atom but could not explain its stability. Bohr introduced discrete allowed energy levels, providing an improved explanation of stable atoms.

Prelims focus

  • Thomson proposed electrons embedded in a positively charged sphere.
  • Rutherford's gold-foil scattering evidence established the nuclear model in 1911.
  • Most alpha particles passed through the foil, showing that most atomic space is empty.
  • Large deflections indicated a small, dense, positively charged nucleus.
  • Bohr proposed discrete permitted electron energy levels in 1913.
  • Trap: Rutherford discovered the nuclear structure, but his model did not explain atomic stability.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class IX, Chapter 4, Structure of the Atom, sections 4.2.1–4.2.3, printed pp. 47–49; American Institute of Physics, Rutherford and the Alpha-Particle Scattering Experiment, consulted 3 November 2026; NobelPrize.org, Niels Bohr, Facts, consulted 3 November 2026.]
